rejected.title: Random and non-random sampling
card: Random sample
every member of the population has an equal chance of being picked, such as drawing names from a hat.
Non-random sample
some members are more likely to be picked than others, such as asking only your friends or only people who volunteer.
Non-random samples can be biased. Bias means the results lean one way and do not fairly show the whole population.
Example: to find the favourite sport of a school of 800, picking 40 names by random draw is fair. Asking only the football team is not, because it leaves out most students.
rejected.remember: Equal chances give a random sample. Unequal chances can make the results biased.

a.q: Which method gives a random sample of the 600 students at a school in Darwin?
opts: Drawing 30 names from a box holding every student's name
Asking the first 30 students to arrive at school
Asking 30 students in the school choir
Asking 30 students who put their hand up
a.why: Only the name draw gives every student an equal chance. Asking the first to arrive is tempting, but early arrivals are a particular group, so others have less chance of being picked.
a.clue: Which method gives every student an equal chance?

b.q: Priya wants to know how often people in her suburb in Perth use the library. She surveys people as they leave the library. Why is her sample likely to be biased?
opts: Library users are more likely to be picked than others
People who rarely visit are more likely to be picked
Everyone in the suburb has the same chance of being picked
Random samples tend to give more biased results
b.why: Only people at the library can be picked, so frequent users have a much greater chance and the results will lean towards them. It is tempting to reverse this, but people who rarely visit are the ones least likely to be at the door.
b.clue: Who could never be picked at the library door?
